entries.title: A Reboot Is Still a Deployment
entries.content:
Most teams I've worked with won't call a deployment finished until the new version has done some real work, such as serving a request or processing a job, and produced the result they expected. A host reboot rarely gets that treatment. The application code hasn't changed, so the restart goes on the maintenance calendar as housekeeping, and the check afterwards is whether the service came back up. I think that bar is too low. What would actually prove that an unchanged service recovered after its host restarted? My answer is a completed job: one piece of the work the service exists to do, finished on the returning host, against the data it's meant to use, and recorded somewhere I can read.

A service runs on a lot more than its code. In a recent Heap article, Guilherme Appel showed how a .NET parallel loop can become serial in a one-CPU container. Lowering the container's limit from two CPUs to one took his 200 records from 42.1 seconds to 83.6, and nobody touched the code. A reboot can change a good deal more than a CPU limit. It can bring back a different kernel, remount the volumes and restart everything on that host the service talks to, in an order its last deployment never tested.

Canonical has changed how often Ubuntu hosts get a new kernel to boot into. On September 23, it announced a new kernel release strategy that replaces its four-week regular and two-week security update cycles with overlapping two-week cycles, so a new kernel ships every week. A new kernel only runs after a reboot, so every one a team installs brings another restart to plan. The Register's report on the new schedule explains that each cycle spends its second week on hardware certification and regression testing. Organizations unwilling to wait, the report adds, can take release candidates after the first week and run their own acceptance tests. That's a sensible offer for the kernel. The acceptance test I'd worry about is the one for the application running on it.

Livepatch moves some of those restarts around without removing them. Canonical describes Livepatch as patching critical and high-severity kernel vulnerabilities "while the system runs." It covers only particular combinations of release, kernel version and flavor, though, and Canonical produces patches for a given kernel for 9 to 13 months after its release, depending on the kernel. After that, its advice is to update and restart. So the restarts still come, on a different schedule.

Decide who owns the unfinished job before shutdown

Picture a team that runs a queue-backed export service on two Linux hosts. Each host runs one worker. A worker takes an export request off the shared queue, writes the finished file to a volume mounted on its host and marks the job done. In this example a job counts as complete only when both of those have happened. In the proposed maintenance window, the host running worker A gets a kernel update and a reboot while worker B stays up on the other host. The service's code stays exactly as it was.

I didn't reboot a server to write this. To see which records an operator would actually have during that window, I built a small rehearsal on a single machine. It runs two worker processes in Python, A and B, which share a SQLite database playing the part of the queue, and the queue holds two jobs, J-001 and J-002. There are no export files in it, only queue rows, and each worker process carries a tag for its run, so A starts out tagged "before." The harness drives the workers by command. An enable command runs a worker's claim gate, the check that decides whether it may take work at all, and a claim command names the job it should try to take. What the rehearsal shows is the order in which the queue records change.

A claimed J-001 first. Then I drained A, which in this harness means one thing: it stops claiming new jobs. When I asked A for J-002, it answered "claims disabled." J-001 was still A's, so before I stopped the process, A put the job back, and the database showed J-001 as queued with no owner.

That requeue is a decision, and I'd want it written into the plan before anyone stops a worker. My harness hands the job back explicitly. A real queue might let the worker finish first, checkpoint partway, or wait for a lease to expire and reassign the job. Each of those changes when J-001 runs next, and whether it starts again from the beginning.

While A was gone, I asked B for J-002, and B claimed it and finished it. I only offered B that one job. Left to itself, a queue would probably have handed B the returned J-001 as well, which is the reason for handing a job back at all. In this run the second worker kept the queue moving, and that's all it shows. Whether one host can carry the whole load is a capacity question, and this rehearsal doesn't touch it.

What worker A showed when it came back

A came back tagged "after," standing in for the rebooted host. Its first line said the process was up. A health check that only looked for a running process would have passed at that point.

When I sent A its enable command, the claim gate looked for a marker file on its volume and read it to confirm the volume was the one it expected. Before the relaunch I had moved the marker away, which is how the rehearsal simulates a volume that didn't come back. The gate reported "dependency unavailable," and a request for J-001 got the same "claims disabled" that J-002 had met during the drain.

I put the marker back and enabled A again. This time the gate opened, and A claimed J-001 and marked it done, with the database recording A as the worker that finished it. In the whole sequence, that row is the first record saying the returned worker did its job.

None of the harness output is a discovery. I wrote the gate, and the harness did what its code says it should. What the rehearsal makes visible is that three records can disagree after a restart: the process said it was up, the gate said its dependency was missing, and no job had finished. The rehearsal is deliberately a narrow check, aiming for the kind of targeted accuracy on one behavior that Sancharini Panda argues a sandbox should have, and it exercised no mount, bootloader or kernel.

On a Linux host, systemd can bring the first two of those records closer together. A unit can list the paths it needs in 

RequiresMountsFor=
, which adds 

Requires=
and 
After=
dependencies on the mount units needed to reach those paths. With a mount unit for the volume, the worker waits for the mount. A service declared as 
Type=notify
 stays in the "starting" state until it sends 
READY=1
, which means the worker decides when its startup is done. The usual default, 
Type=simple
, treats the service as started as soon as its process is forked. For that type, the systemd manual warns, 
systemctl start
will report success "even if the service's binary cannot be invoked successfully."

Even with both settings in place, systemd knows two things: something is mounted at the path, and the worker said it was ready. That second fact is only as good as the worker's own check. In my harness the check is the marker file, and on a real host it should confirm that the mounted volume is the one holding this worker's exports. Neither fact shows that the worker can take a job and record it as finished. That's an application question, and I'd answer it with one representative job.

Rolling back the kernel won't roll back the queue

The obvious shortcut, if the new kernel misbehaves, is to boot the previous one and call that a rollback. I simulated the process-level version. After A finished J-001, I stopped it and relaunched it with the same code and its original tag, "before." The queue still showed J-001 done by A and J-002 done by B.

Each claim and completion in my harness ran as its own committed transaction, and relaunching a process doesn't touch committed rows. Any store with durable commits would behave the same way. SQLite's documentation on atomic commit describes a committed transaction as all or nothing, even across "an operating system crash or power failure."

On the real host, the boot environment and the work are just as separate, and that's where I'd expect a rollback plan to be misread. Booting the previous kernel brings back that kernel. It doesn't bring back packages upgraded in the same window, and it can't reach the queue, the exports already on the volume or anything the worker has sent to another system. If the recovery plan replays jobs after a rollback, and the application has no way to recognize one it already finished, that job can run twice and leave a second copy of the same export.

Who decides when A takes work again

Somebody has to read the J-001 row and decide what happens next, and in more than one incident I've watched, the trouble started when two people each assumed the other one had. Say Dana runs the hosts. She owns the reboot, and afterwards she reports that the host booted and whether the worker's mounts and other dependencies came back. Marcus owns the export service. He sends A one known job while it's still out of normal intake, the way my harness names the job a worker should claim. Then he reads the result and decides when A goes back to ordinary work.

Where that line falls depends on how much of the stack the team controls. If you choose the OS for a bare-metal server yourself, the reboot is yours as well. Atlantic.Net's bare-metal page, for one, says those customers are configured as the system administrator with full root access. Whatever the hosting arrangement, checking that the export service did its job afterwards falls to whoever owns the service, so I'd agree on Dana's half and Marcus's half before the window opens.

Keep the worker out until you can see the result

The condition I'd write into the maintenance plan, before the first worker stops, is that the returning worker completes one representative job against its intended dependency and leaves a result someone other than the worker can check. For the export service, that means a file on the right volume and a queue row naming the worker that finished it. A process that's up, a unit that's active and a mount that's present are all worth seeing on the way there, but none of them is that result.

If the evidence isn't there, A stays out of normal intake, and B keeps the queue moving while Marcus finds out why. Holding A back costs some capacity for as long as that takes. Readmitting a worker that can't do its job costs whatever it touches before anyone notices.

My rehearsal only had the second half of that evidence: one row in a SQLite file, J-001, done, finished by A after its marker file was restored. A real host needs the export file too. With both in hand, that's a reboot I'd sign off on.

entries.title: Agent swarms need more than a message board
entries.summary: Agent swarms are really distributed systems problems in disguise.
entries.content:
Ryan sits down with Vlad Luzin, co-founder and CTO of BAND, to dig into the real engineering challenges underneath the multi-agent hype: why agent swarms are really just distributed systems with non-deterministic microservices, what it actually takes to wire agents together safely at scale, and why your email inbox is now a prompt injection attack surface.

BAND builds the communication infrastructure for multi-agent collaboration—discovery, identity, observability, and sandboxing.

Connect with Vlad on LinkedIn or visit band.ai if you want your agents talking to everyone else's agents.

entries.title: Dispatches from O'Reilly: Inside a software factory
entries.summary: Go from vibe coding to generating clean, maintainable code.
entries.content:
[Ed. note: This article was originally published on O’Reilly Media’s blog, Radar. Republished with permission.]

—————————-

As a software engineer with more than seven years of experience before the coding-agent era, I never liked the idea of vibe coding. But I knew there was a clear line between it and using coding agents to generate clean, maintainable code. That line, where good software principles meet coding agents, is defined by software factories.

That’s why, three months ago, I built my own software factory, Squid, to ship all of Decoding AI’s small and medium projects with minimal human intervention. The first version was so overbuilt I stopped using it.

Meanwhile, I kept seeing people obsess over the next “_____ engineering” label, instead of focusing on actionable outcomes. Prompt engineering, then context engineering, then harness engineering. So far, so good. But in the last few weeks (July 2026 as I write this), things got off track with loop engineering and graph engineering, which already read more like marketing talk than like anything that solves real problems. Graph engineering overtheorizes how teams have built AI applications since the LangGraph era kicked off in ~2024. Don’t get me wrong. The terms aren’t wrong (Boris Cherny, who leads Claude Code at Anthropic, says, “My job is to write loops”), but we’re overexplaining intuitive things we started doing years ago.

While you’re defining what counts as a loop, you’re not thinking about the processes that actually deliver software.

The right frame is the software factory, which was one of the core themes at AI Engineer World’s Fair 2026, where Tereza Tížková (growth at Factory.ai) defined one as “the whole loop, the whole lifecycle of developing software with autonomy.”

I bet you already have an intuitive sense of what a software factory is. In this article, I want to further formalize it and map it onto the software development lifecycle (SDLC). We’ll explore how big your software factory should be, and when to stop automating before it adds more friction than value. Most importantly, I want to highlight where the human belongs in this process, and where I believe they’ll still belong even in a world where all the code is generated by AI.

So…what’s worth automating? Where does the human bring the most value? What’s worth building, and what’s worth buying?

The design of a software factory

Like a physical factory, a software factory automates software creation with minimal human input. Raw work (bug reports, feature ideas, incidents) goes in. Shipped software comes out. It needs a few highly qualified people making high-leverage decisions, and defined gates that work can’t pass through without them.

Factory.ai pitches “a self-improving system for your Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).” Addy Osmani frames the stack as loop, harness, factory: “The loop is the atom”; a factory is “an org chart made of loops.” Warp’s CEO, Zach Lloyd, states that “software engineering will become factory engineering.”

The factory is made up of eight stages that can be divided into three buckets:

What to build. Triage/intake classifies, deduplicates, and routes incoming work. Brainstorming finds high-impact features through market analysis, user data, and technical research. Planning, the most important stage, turns that research into a polished plan, refines it by letting the agent grill you, and tracks decisions in an ADR (Architecture Decision Record) log plus a glossary. The outputs of this stage are tickets backed by documentation that a team of agents can implement, which can be tracked in plain files or a project management tool, such as GitHub Issues, Linear, or Notion.

At this stage, the agent plans in read-only mode, going through the code, the AGENTS.md file, and most importantly the context layer.

Actual building and checking. Implementing is a software engineer and QA agent loop that goes through the tasks and supporting documentation. Review checks the PR diff against product, architecture, and code standards. Review-CI runs the test suite, and failures trigger a fixing agent. Release handles CD to staging/production with human deployment checks.

Self-improving. Monitor/incident response feeds production signals (alerts, errors, incidents) back into triage as fresh input on what to build next, closing the loop.

Orthogonal to the eight stages, we have the context layer. The layer is especially important at the front of the line. Brainstorming is limited to the data it sees: user analytics, competitor analysis, research, transcripts, and documentation. At this stage, a poor context layer directly limits the space of possibilities you can explore. It has a similar impact on planning, where transforming the raw idea into technical specs and tasks depends heavily on how good the examples in the context layer are. If you want to implement a new product-recommendation feature, and you have zero examples, the LLM will just predict the most common thing to do, which often isn’t the best solution for your product.

The context layer can take many forms. One strategy that is becoming increasingly popular is the LLM Wiki, a term coined by Andrej Karpathy. It’s basically a strategy to transform your data into a structured knowledge base, just by using files, instead of a database. Factory, via its AutoWiki feature, transforms popular codebases into a structured knowledge base that agents can query instead of parsing the codebase itself. LangChain recently released OpenWiki, a CLI tool to manage wikis for agent memory. If you’re curious, in this article I detail how I turn my data from Obsidian, Readwise, and Google Drive into agent memory via LLM wikis.

Where the human belongs

To see where the human belongs, let’s walk through the factory with an end-to-end example. We’ll build a feature for a shopping-assistant agent on an ecommerce platform similar to Amazon’s. The scenario is that usage data says users aren’t engaging with its recommendations, and we have to ship an improvement.

Brainstorm is where taste lives. Agents do the grunt work: They analyze user activity, scan competitors’ assistants, and pull research into the knowledge base. Then a member of the technical staff starts looking at the data, understands why people are not engaging with the recommendations, explores how the competition implements their solution, and proposes a fix as a feature spec. At this stage, the spec solves a business problem. It doesn’t need to prescribe a technical solution yet.

Plan is where a human, with the help of the software factory, transforms the feature spec into an implementation plan. Let’s assume that we want to make a change to the recommender engine algorithm. The human chats with the knowledge base, figures out whether it’s feasible, and thinks through architecture, interfaces, data flow, cost, and latency. They then let the agent scan the codebase and grill them until the plan is properly refined into something that fits the codebase. The output is a bunch of tickets plus an ADR explaining the algorithm change and an update to the glossary.

The agent can help within these two stages by quickly scanning through a ton of data and improving the plan, but the human is still central.

Use the strongest model (Fable) for brainstorming and planning. These stages burn fewer tokens than implementation itself, but everything downstream depends on them. A well-written plan lets cheaper models (Opus, Sonnet) execute without reasoning their way out of dead ends. A weak plan makes them retry until the extra tokens erase the price gap.

With a weak plan, I’ve watched Sonnet on high reasoning out-cost Opus on the same task: The smaller model needs more attempts to reach the same goal. Total cost is tokens × price, not model tier. So more failures equals more reasoning, more tokens, and more cost.

From here on, we move into “loop” and “graph” engineering territory.

Implement runs a software engineer agent that picks up every ticket that’s ready to go. As the loop is scoped to a feature, it takes only the associated tickets. After each ticket is implemented, a QA agent tries to find bugs by stress-testing the application. As agents tend to have a positive bias towards their own work, the split between the software engineer and QA agents matters. As Addy Osmani puts it, the model that wrote the code is “way too nice grading its own homework.” This loop, at solo scale, can be as simple as a bunch of terminals pulling tickets. At larger scale, it runs on remote agents working 24/7.

The loop only works if agents can interact with the app. The QA agent needs one command that starts the whole stack reproducibly. From there, it drives the app in the browser, calls the data or fine-tuning pipelines, or hits your server’s API. Whatever your app’s interface is, the agent needs access to it, the same way a human user would.

The key idea is to integrate feedback loops as natively as possible into your software factory. Ideally, you want multiple levels, depending on how expensive it is to run them: linting, unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests. When the loop keeps failing, the root cause is almost always missing plumbing, not the agents.

Review has three steps. Step one checks the product and architecture requirements against the ticket and the ADR. Any discrepancy becomes a new ticket passed back to the implement loop. Step two ensures code quality (modularity, naming) and guards against AI slop such as verbose comments or cryptic function names. Step three looks at the CI/CD pipeline. At every step, any failure auto-creates a task picked up by the software agent.

Not every project needs all three steps. The “factory” ends with a PR that you as a human need to review and merge. But in reality, if you spend enough time creating a strong plan, the PR that reaches you is usually ready to ship as-is.

So where does the human belong? You’re indispensable during brainstorming and planning, and you return for the final check. Agents own everything in between. OpenAI took this to the extreme: ~1M lines and ~1,500 merged PRs over five months with zero hand-written lines. Their framing is “Humans steer. Agents execute.”

Don’t overbuild the factory

With my first Squid version (my own software factory), I got greedy and chased full autonomy: big remote workflows, parallel agents, and one grand pipeline running end to end. It worked, until something went off script. Which it usually does. I couldn’t debug it, couldn’t halt it mid-run, and couldn’t redirect it without throwing the run away. It was a big monolith that took me too far out of the loop, and I couldn’t control it.

I realized you need two options. The first is granular commands that let you grill your plan, implement a specific task, or review one particular step. The second, for when you’re comfortable giving the agent 24/7 autonomy, is an end-to-end command that chains all the smaller ones into a fully autonomous graph, such as one big 

/plan
and 
/implement-review-all command
. Basically, each step is a “loop,” while the whole pipeline is the “graph” of your software factory. Still, note how planning and the rest are split into two different commands, as planning is, and always will be, human-driven (at least if you want the result to stay aligned with what you actually want).

Bottom line. You need to be able to step in, halt it, redirect it, and interrupt it, while still having the option to go fully autonomous.

The bottleneck is me, and that’s by design. To be honest, I’ve worked mostly solo since the AI coding agent boom, and I don’t understand who the people shipping 100 features in parallel are. Most of my features (per project) build on one another, which makes them impossible to parallelize. As the project grows, you can find more and more independent features that can be implemented in parallel, but I still believe that number is limited.

That’s why, when I parallelize, I only use local agents, each running in an isolated codebase via work trees. So far, I’ve never felt the need for 24/7 remote agents, or wanted the overhead of managing them.

A big team can justify more automation, but it has to earn it. So as with any other software product, start small, start by automating the most time-consuming bottlenecks, and add complexity gradually as people get comfortable with the system. Don’t be like me, with my Squid experiment.

Build vs. buy

In all scenarios, you’ll start with a prebuilt coding harness. The most popular vendor-locked ones are Claude Code and Codex. Or go open source with OpenCode or Pi, which took off thanks to its minimalist, extensible architecture that lets you easily build on top of it.

But picking a harness isn’t the same as knowing how to configure it and wire it into your software factory. That’s why everyone needs to know, at least intuitively, how a coding agent works under the hood: the agent loop running in your terminal, what changes when it runs remotely, how you evaluate it, and which context engineering strategies keep it cheap without making it dumber. If you want to learn more about building a coding agent from scratch, consider exploring my open source course on GitHub. Even if you never plan to build your own harness, that intuition is what lets you become a power user.

For a small team, you’ll get extremely far just by defining a set of skills and agents that encode your process on top of the coding harness (a.k.a. your software factory). To keep it simple, this is what I did with Squid, which I use to implement all my projects.

There are other off-the-shelf “software factories” powered just by skills and agents defined in .md files, such as Matt Pocock’s skills repository or the BMad method.

But remember that the factory is mostly about processes, not tools: A factory that doesn’t fit how your team already works adds friction, never gets adopted, and ends up useless.

You cross the buy line the moment engineers you don’t personally supervise run agents. Observability, tracing, cost tracking, and pay-per-token billing stop being optional and become someone’s full-time job. Agent swarms wired into Linear, Slack, and CI across distributed infrastructure are a logistical hell that isn’t your product. That’s when it makes sense to look into off-the-shelf solutions such as Factory.ai (that comes with the Droid agent), or Warp’s Oz. In Warp CEO Zach Lloyd’s words, “Most of the factory is not necessarily a new interface. It is an integration into people’s existing workflows.”

At the other end of the spectrum, you cross back to building when the platform’s constraints cost more than the team it would take to replace it, as OpenAI’s report on its Codex-built product shows.

The smallest builds, the middle buys, and the largest builds again.

What’s next

Someone is already coining next quarter’s “_____ engineering” term as we speak. But the software engineering processes you use to output real code won’t change that often. That’s why you should be open-minded but at the same time focus on actionable outcomes, not on overthinking how to label things.

As Zach Lloyd suggests: Find one “annoying part of your job” and build the smallest loop that handles it.

The harsh reality is that software factories are just at the beginning. They’re far from perfect, and especially far from being fully “autonomous.” Usually, when someone claims they’ve cracked the software factory problem, they either haven’t tested the idea enough or are trying to sell it to you. I’m confident we’ll reach the point where almost the entire software development lifecycle is automated (with the exception of brainstorming and planning), but at the moment we’re still figuring things out.

But here’s what I’m wondering:

Which stage of your factory still needs you the most? I keep automating mine, and the bottleneck stubbornly stays at planning.

Explore next

entries.title: Chaos, then control: the maturity model most AI rollouts skip over
entries.summary: Every engineering org has rolled out AI coding tools by now, but far fewer have actually seen the outcomes they were hoping for.
entries.content:
Every engineering org has rolled out AI coding tools by now, but far fewer have actually seen the outcomes they were hoping for.

Let’s say an organization did the obvious things: bought licenses, ran a lunch-and-learn, unleashed their teams on the new tool. Adoption numbers appear impressive. Nearly everyone touches a coding agent every week. But six months in, they find, the results are wildly uneven. A handful of engineers are doing genuinely different work: taking on projects nobody would’ve attempted before, shipping things on their own that would once have taken a team. But plenty of employees are treating AI as glorified autocomplete: something that exists to make their daily activities slightly faster and easier, not something with the potential to raise the bar in a big way.

That gap isn’t usually diagnosed as a rollout problem. It’s identified as a talent problem (“I guess some people are just better with these tools than others”) or a tooling issue (“If only we had better tools”). But the real problem is that most orgs skip a crucial stage in AI rollouts: the part where chaos is tamed and codified into a system.

A borrowed line, a real sequence

Vivek Raghunathan, SVP of engineering at Snowflake, opened a recent Leaders of Code conversation with a maxim borrowed from Intel’s Andy Grove: During any platform shift, you have to let chaos reign before you can rein in the chaos. The implication is that these are two distinct phases with two distinct jobs. Jumping into the second one before the first one is finished doesn’t save time; it just produces a rollout that performs like a coin flip. Will it work? Who knows!

Raghunathan’s team built their AI rollout as a five-stage progression:

  1. Let chaos reign.
  2. Discover what actually works.
  3. Codify it into a shared language.
  4. Rein in the chaos by scaling that language across the org.
  5. Reorganize around the new reality.

Crucially, step 5 cannot take place until the previous four stages have done their work. Most companies, understandably eager to show a return on the tools they’ve bought, compress or skip straight past stages two and three. They mandate a tool, then jump to expecting consistent gains without ever building the connective tissue that turns individual competence into organizational knowledge.

What the skipped stages actually look like

Measuring the wrong thing, too early. It’s tempting to judge an AI rollout on hard numbers right away: lines of code, PRs merged, tickets closed. Raghunathan’s team set out to avoid this, operating on the assumption that those metrics are easy to game and don’t tell you whether people are getting better at using the tools. In the “let chaos reign” phase, the only metric that matters is adoption itself: Are people actually using it? Are they using it for more than one kind of task? Everything else is noise until you know what “good” looks like.

No shared vocabulary for what’s working. This is the stage most rollouts skip entirely. Once people are experimenting, some of them build (or stumble onto) genuinely better ways of working. But if nobody’s watching for those successful experiments, they can stay locked in individual heads. Raghunathan’s team intentionally went looking for them by asking engineers about the best practices they’d developed in their own work. They ended up with roughly 14 named patterns, including: plan in writing before you write code, fence your agents into separate git worktrees so parallel work doesn’t collide, keep an orchestrating agent free of heavy context so it can delegate instead of getting bogged down. The names matter less than the fact that they exist at all: a pattern language, deliberately modeled on the “Gang of Four” software design patterns, gives a team something concrete to teach and measure themselves against.

Scaling by mandate instead of by mechanism. Once you have a set of practices that actually work, the instinct is to announce them and expect adoption: a mandate. Raghunathan’s team instead built a mechanism: regular “focus weeks,” where the entire org sets aside dedicated time to catch up on the paved path or to forge past it. That approach works because it’s a structural answer to a structural problem: You can’t tell people to internalize new habits during the same overloaded sprint cadence you had before AI showed up.

Reorganizing before the previous steps are done. The last stage—changing how roles, responsibilities, and org charts actually work—is the one everyone wants to talk about first, because it’s the most visible and the most dramatic. But it comes last for a reason. It sounds obvious once you say it, but you can’t sensibly redesign a role around AI-assisted work until you know what AI-assisted work reliably looks like at your company. (The proverbial cart preceded by horse comes to mind.) Skipping ahead to this stage usually leads to restructuring around guesses.

Why organizations skip the middle

These steps aren’t skipped because business leaders don’t understand that adoption does not automatically equal mastery. It’s because those middle stages are unglamorous and genuinely hard to run.

Discovery doesn’t feel like progress. Watching what your best people are doing, then naming and sharing it out, doesn’t lend itself to a press release the way “we rolled out Tool X org-wide” does. It’s slower, less visible, and easy to deprioritize when there’s pressure to show a return on a big tooling investment.

Codifying practice requires someone to go looking. Raghunathan describes actively seeking out the “fearless explorers” in his org and getting them to explain what they’ve found. It sounds simple, but in practice many organizations stumble here. You need a real time investment from someone senior enough to translate their findings into something teachable. It also feels skippable when everyone’s plate is already full.

It’s tempting to treat the tool as the whole answer. Buying licenses is a decision you can make once. Building a pattern language, then a mechanism to spread it, then eventually a new org structure, is an ongoing practice. And it’s much harder to build a practice than it is to make a purchase.

What running the sequence actually looks like

Resist grading the rollout before you understand the range. In the early months, track whether people are using the tools across a range of tasks—writing and reviewing code, drafting design docs—rather than whether output metrics have moved. A wide range of outcomes at this stage isn’t a failure signal; it’s raw material you need to inform stage two.

Go looking for what’s already working, on purpose. Somewhere in your org, a handful of people have already figured out something non-obvious. Find them, and get specific about what they’re actually doing differently. That specificity is what turns a one-off into a pattern.

Give the pattern language a name and a distribution mechanism. A list of best practices in an unread wiki won’t spread throughout the org. To do that, you need a dedicated block of time, whether it’s a recurring practice session or a focus week like Raghunathan’s team used, where people are expected to learn the paved path or do some trailblazing of their own.

Hold off on the org chart. The instinct to redesign roles and responsibilities around AI is understandable, but keep in mind that they’re the payoff of the first four stages, not a shortcut past them. An org chart built on last quarter’s guesses about how AI-assisted work would go is going to need rebuilding anyway.

The step you can’t skip

Remember the team from the intro: near-universal adoption, wildly uneven results, no clear understanding of why. The tools aren’t the problem, and neither are the individual team members. The absence of a middle stage—the unglamorous work of discovering, naming, and deliberately spreading what actually works—is the real problem. Skipping the middle stage produces the gap between, on one hand, engineers who are much more productive and creative with AI on board, and on the other, folks using a more sophisticated version of autocomplete.

Letting chaos reign is the easy part. Organizations do it by mandating a tool and stepping back. Reining in that chaos is the part that takes actual management: finding what’s working, giving it a name, and building a mechanism to spread it before you reach for the org chart.

If your rollout has adoption numbers but no shared vocabulary for what “good” looks like, which stage are you actually in—and is anyone responsible for getting you to the next one?
